hook: A whole New England town is the anomaly here, or rather what is left of it after a few days nobody outside could see into. The file is assembled from scraps: expedition radio logs, security footage, diaries, a shopping list and a preacher's notes. Content note: the description of the aftermath is grim and includes self-inflicted deaths and violence, though it is written as a detached inventory.
whyItMatters:
This is a good example of an entry built like a disaster scrapbook rather than a single report. You never get a clean account of what happened; you reconstruct it from fragments, the way the Foundation has to.

It is also notable for its tone. Real dread sits right next to deliberate absurdity, from a mural full of oddly specific minor gods to a footnote about a song that should not exist yet. Readers tend to either love that mix or find it jarring, and both reactions are part of the experience.
thingsToNotice:
Watch the name that keeps appearing in unexpected places, signed under an apology and later burned into stone. It is the closest thing the article has to a hero, and it is never explained.

The cult's documents move from mundane to unhinged: an errand list with grumbling asides, then a journal that grows less steady, then a speech, then the back cover. Reading them in order shows how the article lets its villain undo himself through his own writing. The expedition log is worth a second look too, because one small footnote about who noticed an inconsistency, and when, quietly sets the rules for the mist.

related.note: Another file mostly told through recovered transmissions, in a far gentler key.
